title: Divisibility, Factors & Multiples
weightage: High — divisibility, GCD and LCM feed remainders, fractions, ratios and word problems
intro: Divisibility is the machinery behind a surprising number of GRE questions — not just "is this divisible by 3?" but fractions that must simplify, ratios that must reduce, and word problems about events that line up on a schedule. A factor divides a number evenly; a multiple is what you get by multiplying it. The two ideas that pay off most are the greatest common divisor (GCD, also called HCF) and the least common multiple (LCM): GCD is about splitting things into equal groups, LCM is about when repeating cycles coincide. Learn the quick divisibility tests, and you will do in your head what the on-screen basic calculator would make slow and error-prone.

topics.name: Divisibility Rules
topics.details: Divisibility tests let you decide whether one number divides another without doing the division. The high-value ones: a number is divisible by 2 if its last digit is even; by 3 if the sum of its digits is a multiple of 3; by 4 if its last two digits form a multiple of 4; by 5 if it ends in 0 or 5; by 9 if its digit sum is a multiple of 9; and by 6 if it passes both the 2-test and the 3-test at once. For composite divisors, split into coprime parts and test each — divisibility by 12 means divisible by 3 and by 4. These tests turn a slow calculator entry into a two-second mental check, which matters because the GRE calculator is deliberately basic. The digit-sum tests (3 and 9) are the ones test-takers most often forget, yet they appear constantly.

solved.problem: Is 5,742 divisible by 3?
solved.solution: Digit sum = 5 + 7 + 4 + 2 = 18, which is a multiple of 3. So yes, 5,742 is divisible by 3.

solved.problem: Is 1,236 divisible by 4?
solved.solution: Check only the last two digits: 36. Since 36 = 4 × 9, the whole number is divisible by 4. Yes.

solved.problem: The number 3,4_6 is divisible by 9. What is the missing digit?
solved.solution: Digit sum = 3 + 4 + d + 6 = 13 + d must be a multiple of 9. The nearest is 18, so d = 5. The number is 3,456.

solved.problem: Quantitative Comparison. n is divisible by 6. Quantity A: the remainder when n is divided by 3. Quantity B: the remainder when n is divided by 2. Which is greater?
solved.solution: Divisible by 6 means divisible by both 2 and 3, so both remainders are 0. Quantity A = Quantity B = 0; they are equal.

unsolved.problem: What digit d makes 47d divisible by 5?

topics.name: Factors & Multiples
topics.details: A factor (or divisor) of n divides n with no remainder; a multiple of n is n times an integer. Factors of a positive integer are finite and paired — for 24 the pairs are (1,24), (2,12), (3,8), (4,6) — while multiples go on forever: 24, 48, 72, … . The GRE leans on three facts. First, the smallest factor of any n > 1 is 1 and the largest is n itself. Second, every factor of n is at most n, and every multiple of n is at least n (for positive n). Third, if a is a factor of b and b is a factor of c, then a is a factor of c. A common wording trap: "factor" and "multiple" are opposites — 4 is a factor of 12, and 12 is a multiple of 4. Read which direction the question wants before you answer.

solved.problem: List all positive factors of 36.
solved.solution: Pair them up: 1×36, 2×18, 3×12, 4×9, 6×6. So the factors are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36 — nine factors (the repeated 6 counts once, because 36 is a perfect square).

solved.problem: What is the smallest multiple of 7 that is greater than 100?
solved.solution: 100 ÷ 7 ≈ 14.3, so 7 × 15 = 105 is the first multiple above 100.

solved.problem: If 12 is a factor of n, list three facts that must be true about n.
solved.solution: n is a multiple of 12, so n is also divisible by every factor of 12 — in particular by 2, 3, 4 and 6. And n ≥ 12 (for positive n).

solved.problem: Quantitative Comparison. Quantity A: the number of positive factors of 12. Quantity B: the number of positive factors of 18. Which is greater?
solved.solution: Factors of 12: 1,2,3,4,6,12 → 6 factors. Factors of 18: 1,2,3,6,9,18 → 6 factors. They are equal.

unsolved.problem: What is the largest factor of 45 other than 45 itself?
hints: Largest proper factor = n / smallest prime.

unsolved.problem: How many multiples of 6 are there between 1 and 50?
If n is a multiple of 15, must it be a multiple of 5?

topics.name: GCD (HCF)
topics.details: The greatest common divisor GCD(a, b) — also called the highest common factor, HCF — is the largest integer that divides both a and b. The reliable method is prime factorisation: take each shared prime raised to its lowest power. For 48 = 2⁴·3 and 60 = 2²·3·5, the common primes are 2 (lowest power 2²) and 3, so GCD = 4 × 3 = 12. GCD answers "what is the largest equal group I can make?" — the biggest identical bundles, the largest square tile that fits a rectangle exactly, or the largest number of gift bags with the same contents. If two numbers share no prime factors, their GCD is 1 and they are called coprime (or relatively prime), which is exactly the condition for a fraction to be fully reduced.

solved.problem: Find GCD(48, 60).
solved.solution: 48 = 2⁴·3 and 60 = 2²·3·5. Take shared primes at the lowest power: 2² and 3¹. GCD = 4 × 3 = 12.

solved.problem: A florist has 24 roses and 36 tulips and wants identical bunches using all flowers. What is the greatest number of bunches?
solved.solution: The greatest equal split is GCD(24, 36). 24 = 2³·3, 36 = 2²·3². GCD = 2²·3 = 12. So 12 bunches (each with 2 roses and 3 tulips).

solved.problem: Reduce 84/126 to lowest terms.
Quantitative Comparison. Quantity A: GCD(15, 28). Quantity B: 1. Which is greater?
solved.solution: 15 = 3·5 and 28 = 2²·7 share no prime factors, so GCD = 1. They are coprime. Quantity A = Quantity B = 1; equal.

unsolved.problem: Largest square tile (whole cm) that exactly tiles a 60 cm by 48 cm floor?

topics.name: LCM
topics.details: The least common multiple LCM(a, b) is the smallest positive integer that both a and b divide into. By prime factorisation, take each prime that appears in either number raised to its highest power. For 12 = 2²·3 and 18 = 2·3², use 2² and 3², giving LCM = 4 × 9 = 36. LCM answers "when do repeating cycles line up?" — two buses that leave every 12 and 18 minutes next depart together after 36 minutes; it is also the right common denominator when adding fractions. Contrast it with GCD: GCD is at most the smaller number, LCM is at least the larger. The GRE frequently disguises LCM as a scheduling or "meet again" word problem, so when two independent cycles must coincide, reach for LCM.

solved.problem: Find LCM(12, 18).
solved.solution: 12 = 2²·3, 18 = 2·3². Take the highest power of each prime: 2² and 3². LCM = 4 × 9 = 36.

solved.problem: Two lighthouses flash every 8 and 12 seconds and just flashed together. When do they next flash together?
solved.solution: They coincide at LCM(8, 12). 8 = 2³, 12 = 2²·3, so LCM = 2³·3 = 24. Next simultaneous flash: 24 seconds later.

solved.problem: What is the smallest number divisible by 4, 5 and 6?
Quantitative Comparison. Quantity A: LCM(6, 8). Quantity B: 6 × 8. Which is greater?
solved.solution: LCM(6, 8) = 24 (since 6 = 2·3, 8 = 2³ → 2³·3). 6 × 8 = 48. Quantity B is greater — the product overshoots because 6 and 8 share the factor 2.

unsolved.problem: Trains leave every 15 and 25 minutes together at 9:00. Next joint departure?

topics.name: GCD–LCM Relationship
topics.details: For any two positive integers, GCD and LCM are tied by one clean identity: GCD(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b. This lets you find one from the other without listing anything — if you know a, b and the GCD, then LCM = (a × b)/GCD. It also acts as a sanity check: the GCD must divide the LCM, and both a and b must be multiples of the GCD and factors of the LCM. Note the identity is a two-number rule; it does not extend to three numbers as GCD × LCM = product. A neat consequence the GRE tests: if two numbers are coprime (GCD = 1), their LCM is simply their product. Knowing this relationship converts several "find the other quantity" questions into a single division.

solved.problem: Two numbers have GCD 6 and LCM 72. If one is 24, find the other.
solved.solution: GCD × LCM = product: 6 × 72 = 432. The other number = 432 / 24 = 18.

solved.problem: Verify the identity for 12 and 18.
solved.solution: GCD(12,18) = 6, LCM(12,18) = 36. Product of the identity: 6 × 36 = 216 = 12 × 18. It checks out.

solved.problem: The GCD of two numbers is 8 and their LCM is 96. What is the product of the numbers?
solved.solution: By the identity, product = GCD × LCM = 8 × 96 = 768.

solved.problem: Quantitative Comparison. a and b are coprime positive integers. Quantity A: LCM(a, b). Quantity B: a × b. Which is greater?
solved.solution: Coprime means GCD = 1, so LCM = (a × b)/1 = a × b. Quantity A = Quantity B; they are equal.

unsolved.problem: GCD is 4, LCM is 48, one number is 16. Find the other.
Two numbers are 14 and 21. Find LCM using the identity.
If GCD × LCM = 360 and the GCD is 6, what is the LCM?

shortcuts: Digit-sum tests are your fastest friends: divisible by 3 (or 9) iff the digit sum is. The GRE calculator can never beat this.
For a composite divisor, split into coprime parts: by 12 = by 3 AND by 4; by 15 = by 3 AND by 5.
GCD = shared primes at the LOWEST power; LCM = all primes at the HIGHEST power. Say it that way and you never mix them up.
GCD × LCM = a × b. Know any three of {a, b, GCD, LCM} and the fourth is one division away.
Coprime (GCD = 1) ⇒ LCM = a × b. Spot coprimality and skip the factorisation.
"Largest equal groups / biggest tile" → GCD. "When do cycles coincide / smallest common amount" → LCM.
mistakes: Swapping GCD and LCM — taking highest powers for the GCD or lowest for the LCM.
Applying GCD × LCM = product to THREE numbers. The identity holds for two numbers only.
Testing divisibility by 4 using the whole number instead of just the last two digits (same for 8 → last three).
Forgetting that a perfect square (like 36) has an odd number of factors because one pair repeats.
Reading "factor" as "multiple". 4 is a factor of 12; 12 is a multiple of 4 — opposite directions.
Assuming two even numbers are coprime. They always share the factor 2, so GCD ≥ 2.

pyq.q: Quantitative Comparison — Quantity A: GCD(a, b). Quantity B: LCM(a, b), for positive integers a, b. Which is greater?
pyq.a: Quantity B. The GCD never exceeds the smaller number and the LCM is never smaller than the larger, so LCM ≥ GCD always (equal only when a = b).

pyq.q: A scheduling problem: Bus X every 20 min, Bus Y every 30 min, both leave at 8:00. When do they next leave together?
pyq.a: LCM(20, 30) = 60 min, so 9:00. Any "meet/leave together again" cue points to LCM.

pyq.q: Numeric Entry — a rectangle 90 cm by 120 cm is tiled by identical square tiles with whole-cm sides, using the fewest tiles. Enter the tile side.
pyq.a: Fewest tiles means the LARGEST square, i.e. GCD(90, 120) = 30 cm.

pyq.q: Multiple-answer — which of 2, 3, 4, 6, 9 must divide any integer divisible by 36? Select all.
pyq.a: All of them. 36 = 2²·3², so every factor of 36 — including 2, 3, 4, 6 and 9 — divides any multiple of 36.

summary: Divisibility tests (2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9) replace slow calculator division with mental checks.
Factors are finite and paired; multiples are infinite; the two words point in opposite directions.
GCD = shared primes at lowest powers; it answers "largest equal group / biggest tile".
LCM = all primes at highest powers; it answers "when do cycles coincide / smallest common amount".
GCD × LCM = a × b for two numbers — find any one of the four from the other three.
Coprime numbers have GCD 1, so their LCM is just the product.
Split composite divisibility into coprime parts (12 = 3 and 4).
On GRE word problems, "equal groups" signals GCD and "meet again" signals LCM.
